## Appendix D $\upchi$ -Bench detail

### D.1 Task construction details

#### Difficulty definitions.

Each domain uses a structurally grounded difficulty signal. Provider PA difficulty is the count of distinct document kinds the submission packet must carry to satisfy the payer-published per-procedure document list: Easy = 0 required document kinds, Moderate = 1–3, Hard = $\geq 4$ . Payer UM difficulty is the number of clinical criteria along the chosen path through the payer’s policy decision tree: Easy = $\leq 5$ criteria, Moderate = 6–9, Hard = $\geq 10$ . Care management difficulty maps one-to-one to the patient persona’s consent profile: Engaged = Easy, Hesitant = Moderate, Refusing = Hard.

#### Task generation pipeline.

Step 1 of Section 3.2.2 is implemented as a rejection-sampling loop around an LLM agent generator (Claude Opus 4.7 with JSON-schema-constrained output). The generator is forbidden from emitting any field that is not anchored to a citation in (i) or (ii); each rubric line and each required chart fact carries an explicit pointer back to a policy section or NNN node, so a candidate that omits citations is rejected at parse time.

Acceptance criteria A candidate must pass three gates before it is queued for human review. (G1) every expected action and rubric line resolves to a cited section or NNN node. (G2) chart and rubric mutually entail and the chosen path does not appear verbatim in chart prose, so the rubric cannot be passed by surface paraphrase. (G3) a deterministic dry-run executes a reference solution to a single well-formed terminal state, with reference-solution length, decision-tree depth, and irreversible-commit count falling inside one of the three difficulty bands. G1–G2 failures are looped back to the generator with the failed-gate diagnostic, up to three retries; G3 failures are discarded.

These gates filtered 523 candidates down to 172 tasks for human review. After human review, we further balanced the dataset by difficulty, type of diagnosis, and initial/final states to create the final 75-task benchmark.

Human review and clinician editing (Step 3 in Section 3.2.2). Outsourced licensed clinicians review and edit each surviving candidate; chart authors work blinded to the per-stage ground-truth bundle to prevent phrasing overlap that would let the rubric grade prose rather than evidence. Reviewers re-couple chart and rubric during review and rewrite any field whose wording would shortcut the policy-navigation task. The same review pass also runs the residual-PHI scan and the clinical-realism check (“would a real reviewer encounter this case?”); a candidate that fails either is sent back for rewrite or, on a second failure, dropped.

#### Validation composition.

The review panel for each task combines (i) at least one practicing healthcare worker with the credential appropriate to the role under review (RN for nurse-review and CM rubrics, MD for physician-review and P2P rubrics, RN/MD for PA documentation rubrics), (ii) a separate clinician operating the $\upchi$ -World UI to confirm tractability under the role’s tool surface, and (iii) five paper authors covering the policy-text, simulator-state, and rubric-coverage perspectives. Chart authors are kept blinded to the per-stage GT bundle so chart prose cannot mirror rubric phrasing; the panel re-couples chart and rubric only at sign-off. Disagreements are resolved by majority vote; clinical disagreements that survive a vote escalate to a board-certified arbiter. A formal per-task human inter-rater statistic is not reported here because reviewer-level verdicts were logged only as accept/reject decisions rather than per-rubric Likert votes.

### D.2 Prior authorization and utilization management

#### Clinical categories.

Payer UM tasks span five high-level clinical categories chosen to exercise a breadth of policy types that routinely generate prior-authorization requests in commercial managed care, while keeping each category anchored to concrete, widely-recognized procedures that allow policy lookup to be unambiguous. Each category is grounded in one to three specific CPT/HCPCS-indexed procedures drawn from real payer medical policies; see Table 10 for the per-category task counts.

Provider PA tasks are categorized by their terminal status rather than clinical procedure, because the benchmark focuses on the provider’s documentation and submission behavior rather than the clinical determination itself. Three terminal states are covered: Submitted to payer (8), where the agent assembles and submits a complete packet; Returned for docs (12), where the submission is incomplete and the agent must identify and retrieve the missing document kinds; Gather more evidence (5), where the clinical record lacks information needed to satisfy the payer’s coverage criteria and the agent must coordinate with the ordering clinician before a formal submission is possible.

#### Policy criteria structure (Payer UM).

Each UM task is grounded in a specific payer medical policy and encodes the set of criteria applicable to the requested service. Each criterion is a triplet: (i) criterion text, the natural-language condition transcribed verbatim from the policy; (ii) policy citation, the exact section identifier and version the agent must name when recording its evaluation; and (iii) evidence items, chart-specific facts that demonstrate how the criterion is (or is not) met for this particular patient case.

The citation requirement is a core design choice: the LLM judge cannot award a positive verdict for clinically plausible reasoning that fails to reference the applicable policy section by name. Each criterion has a rollup rule (all items or any item) that mirrors the policy’s own aggregation logic.

Difficulty tracks the length of the applicable policy path. Easy tasks ( $\leq$ 5 criteria) correspond to routing decisions that resolve on administrative grounds or minimal documentation checks. Moderate tasks (6–9 criteria) cover standard single-procedure reviews with complete documentation and medical-necessity evaluation. Hard tasks ( $\geq$ 10 criteria) arise from multi-page surgical policies or cases with comorbidity exclusion checks, cumulative evidence requirements, and multiple decision nodes.

#### Document status classification (Provider PA).

Each PA task encodes the payer handbook’s per-procedure document requirement as a list of required document kinds (e.g., chart_note, imaging_report, progress_note). Before submission, the agent must determine the status of each required kind in the patient’s document repository. Documents fall into one of three status categories that determine the correct agent behavior.

Present and sufficient: a document of the required kind exists and its content satisfies the policy’s minimum content criteria. The agent should attach it to the submission packet without modification. Present but insufficient: a document of the required kind exists, but its content fails the policy’s requirements (e.g., a therapy evaluation note that lacks standardized assessment scores or measurable functional goals). The agent must identify the insufficiency, communicate the gap to the ordering provider, and obtain a supplementary document or addendum before submission can proceed. Absent: no document of the required kind exists in the repository. The agent cannot assemble a valid submission packet and must coordinate with the ordering clinician to gather the missing clinical evidence upstream.

#### Workflow design.

UM tasks are seeded at one of the five pickup stages rather than uniformly at Intake, testing agents’ ability to pick up a case mid-workflow, as happens when cases are reassigned to a new reviewer or escalated after hours. The initial-stage distribution (Nurse review 8, Intake 5, Physician review 4, Triage 4, Peer-to-peer 4) is weighted toward more complex review stages to concentrate evaluations on clinically demanding decisions. All four terminal outcomes (Approved (9), Denied (10), Pended (5), Coverage not required (1)) are represented, preventing any bias toward a single determination type.

Tasks traverse two to five review stages ( $n_{\text{stages}}\in\{2,3,4,5\}$ ), capturing both direct determinations (2 stages: review + letter delivery) and fully escalated chains (5 stages: intake through peer-to-peer). The number of clinical criteria along the policy decision path ranges from 0 to 50 (mean 9.2), where zero-criteria cases correspond to non-clinical routing decisions (e.g., coverage not required at triage) and high-criteria cases reflect complex multi-page surgical policies.

Table 10 cross-tabulates initial stage against terminal state. The Gather more evidence column is absent from the UM table because that terminal state applies only to Provider PA tasks.

#### Peer-to-peer simulation.

Four UM tasks (16%) are seeded at the Peer-to-peer stage. This stage is operationally distinct: the payer has already issued a preliminary denial, the requesting provider has contested it and requested a clinical peer review, and the agent must now defend or revise its determination in a live multi-turn call against the provider’s attending physician. The clinical counterpart, played by the simulation environment, advocates for the provider’s position using chart-grounded arguments and may surface clinical details not foregrounded in the prior review.

All four P2P tasks resolve to either Approved (2) or Denied (2); a Pended outcome is structurally excluded because the call must resolve the case.

#### Evaluation design.

UM and PA tasks are scored by a two-layer verifier. The deterministic layer reads the simulator’s persisted world state and event log and checks: (i) terminal case status; (ii) routing and review-lane assignments; (iii) per-stage structured payloads, including criterion-by-criterion evaluations, decision-and-rationale fields, completeness flags; (iv) required side-effect artifacts (determination letters, information-request notices); and (v) mutation scope, where writes to cases or patients outside the task’s designated scope count as failures. The LLM-judge layer reads the same persisted records and grades, per workflow stage: whether clinical reasoning is grounded in policy sections cited by name; whether criterion evaluations are internally consistent and align with the chart evidence; and whether the terminal determination follows from the recorded rationale. All judge rubrics inline the specific policy-section citations they require, so that a verdict cannot be awarded by plausible-sounding language alone. Both layers must return a positive verdict for a trial to count as a pass.

### D.3 Care management

#### Workflow design.

The care management workflow follows the five-phase RN case management process used in commercial chronic-disease and complex-care programs: (i) Intake: confirm the referral, verify program eligibility, assign a risk tier, and open the case; (ii) Chart review: extract diagnoses, lab trends, medication history, recent encounters, and social determinants of health from the longitudinal record; (iii) Outreach: contact the patient by phone, establish rapport, confirm consent, and conduct a structured assessment interview; (iv) Formal assessment: administer the four-domain assessment instruments (see Table 7 for the full instrument set) grounded in the chart and the outreach transcript; (v) Care plan authoring and closure: document NANDA-I nursing diagnoses, NOC outcome targets, and NIC interventions grounded in chart findings and assessment results, then either finalize the plan or close the case. Disenrollment is a side path that may fire at any earlier phase when the patient refuses, is unreachable, or a safety concern surfaces.

Care plans are required to follow the NANDA-I/NOC/NIC (NNN) framework because this is the documentation standard for RN care management in U.S. managed-care programs. Each task is designed so that the ground-truth care plan requires a minimum of two NANDA-I diagnoses with corresponding NOC targets and NIC interventions, drawn from the per-condition NNN model.

#### Patient simulation.

Each patient persona is a structured contract with four interlocking components.

Consent triggers are explicit caller behaviors that advance the patient’s trust state. The LLM judge evaluates whether a given agent turn matches each trigger’s natural-language specification. An agent applying standard clinical intake workflows without adapting to the patient’s stated boundaries will not accumulate the required triggers and cannot obtain same-call consent.

Anti-triggers are behaviors that damage rapport, some permanently closing off consent or specific disclosure paths for the remainder of the call. Anti-triggers are specified in natural language with handbook section citations so the LLM judge can evaluate them independently of surface phrasing. For Refusing patients who require all T-rules to fire with zero A-rules, a single poorly-chosen phrase closes the consent path permanently.

Consent rules specify the gating threshold: the minimum combination of triggers fired and anti-triggers avoided for the patient to grant same-call enrollment consent. Thresholds scale with difficulty: Engaged patients require 1–2 triggers; Refusing patients require all T-rules with zero A-rules. Without the consent flag set, the agent cannot administer any formal assessment instrument.

Assessment disclosure rules govern which clinical information the patient will share during the outreach conversation, and when. Before the patient will disclose on a gated topic, the caller must: (i) explain why this topic matters; (ii) acknowledge the patient’s right to skip or stop; (iii) state any applicable safety limits. Bundled checklist questions, chart assumptions, or three or more sensitive domains in one turn trigger partial withdrawal and deferral of non-gated items. Patient engagement profiles span three consent stances (Engaged (3 tasks), Hesitant (7), and Refusing (15)), mapping one-to-one to Easy, Moderate, and Hard difficulty. Primary conditions span 22 single-condition primaries and 3 multimorbidity scenarios across 8 clinical categories. The four program types (Chronic disease (11), Behavioral health (6), Complex care (4), Transitions of care (4)) map to distinct operational playbooks in the care-manager sub-skill.

Table 11 lists all 25 tasks with their primary condition, category, program type, consent profile, and difficulty.

#### Evaluation design.

CM tasks are scored by the same two-layer verifier as PA/UM, with adaptations for the nursing process. The deterministic layer checks: (i) forward-only state-machine progression through the five phases; (ii) the consent-obtained completeness flag, which must be set before any assessment instrument can be administered; (iii) care-plan structural completeness, where at least two NANDA-I diagnoses, each linked to NOC targets and NIC interventions, must be present; and (iv) field-level completeness for all administered structured instruments. The LLM-judge layer grades: (i) engagement appropriateness, i.e., whether the communication style matches the patient’s consent profile and respects its resistance triggers; (ii) assessment grounding, i.e., whether each instrument response is traceable to chart evidence or to the outreach transcript; (iii) care-plan composition, i.e., whether each NNN entry is supported by chart or transcript evidence and aligns with the per-condition NNN model; and (iv) escalation judgment, i.e., whether red-flag conditions are correctly identified and routed.

### E.1 Sandbox environment and trial orchestrator

Each trial in $\upchi$ -Bench is materialized as a containerized sandbox bound to a single task, layered over a shared $\upchi$ -World: one fixed population of data of all 25 tasks in the domain. The sandbox33 3 During experiments, we hosted the sandbox on Modal [35]. carries its own per-trial database, file system, and tool-server processes, and is shut down after the trial returns so no state is shared across trials. At trial start, the $\upchi$ -World backend, the role-scoped MCP servers [3], and the agent process are brought up in parallel; the simulator composes the shared world with the task manifest to pin a specific task to its initial state. The agent communicates with the simulator exclusively through MCP over streamable HTTP. Harbor [18, 34] sits between the two as the trial orchestrator: it spawns and tears down the sandbox, wires up the agent–simulator MCP channel, records the agent’s step trajectory, and enforces the per-trial wall-clock and retry budget.

### E.2 Pass@k and pass^k metrics

For each task we run $n=3$ independent trials and let $c\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ count the passes. From the same pool we compute task-level pass@ $k$ and pass^ $k$ :

$$ \mathrm{pass@}k\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,1-\binom{n-c}{k}\big/\binom{n}{k}\,\right],\qquad\mathrm{pass}^{k}\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\binom{c}{k}\big/\binom{n}{k}\,\right]. $$

pass^ $3$ is the operationally meaningful reliability number, since long-horizon healthcare workflows must succeed on every individual case rather than admit a single successful sample. Setting $n{=}k{=}3$ keeps pass^ $3$ a defined reliability signal at a tractable budget: $30\text{ cells}\times 75\text{ tasks}\times 3\text{ trials}=6{,}750$ trials per benchmark pass.

### E.3 Judge, container, and harness configuration

The rubric judge is Claude Opus 4.7, capped at a 1200-second wall-clock and 128K output tokens per rubric. Each rubric is judged by $V=3$ independent votes that are aggregated under a strict-majority quorum (ties resolved as fail); inter-rater agreement statistics computed on this $V$ -fold voting record are reported below. Per-trial container resources are identical across all (harness, model) cells: 2 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM, 10 GB ephemeral disk. For all tasks, we set an agent wall-clock cap of 1800 s, which is roughly twice the P99 of wall-clock time of Claude Opus 4.7 on all tasks during preliminary experiments. Per-harness turn caps and agent sampling parameters are inherited from defaults except for the OpenAI Agents SDK, which we pin to its upstream-reference setting of 50 turns; we deliberately do not override sampling so that each loop is measured as users encounter it. A trial that exhausts wall-clock without reaching a verifier-resolvable terminal state is counted as a failure for both pass@ $k$ and pass^ $k$ .

### E.4 OpenAI Agents SDK harness customization

We keep the upstream loop intact (the SDK’s Runner.run drives turn dispatch and tool selection) and limit our customizations to four areas, all listed for completeness because they are load-bearing for reproducibility rather than algorithmic. (i) Loop bounds are exposed as harness flags max_turns (default 50, the upstream-reference value), max_retries (10), and max_tool_return_chars (100K). (ii) MCP integration surfaces the role-scoped MCP servers through MCPServerStreamableHttp with cache_tools_list=True, plus a sanitizer that rewrites dotted MCP tool names into the OpenAI function-name regex ˆ[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$. (iii) Oversize tool outputs are spilled to disk via a MCPUtil.invoke_mcp_tool wrapper: results above the 100K char budget are written to overlong_tool_outputs/ and replaced in the LLM-visible payload with a head plus a file-pointer the agent can re-read. (iv) Telemetry / retries use the SDK 0.13.6 ModelRetrySettings pipeline (network errors, HTTP 408/409/425/429/5xx, Retry-After, exponential backoff with jitter) so transient transport failures do not count as task failures. The default “stop on tool error” behavior is left untouched. The system prompt is the verbatim Toolathlon general_v0 template; the eight built-in tools match the implicit capability set of the first-party CLIs.

#### Verifier robustness and judge bias.

We treat Table 18 as a within-judge stability check, not a cross-judge validation: $V=3$ self-agreement of Claude Opus 4.7 cannot rule out same-family bias from the judge being part of the evaluated model family. We mitigate this in three ways. (i) Deterministic anchor. Every rubric pass is conditioned on the deterministic contract also passing ( $R_{T}=\mathrm{DeterministicPass}\land\mathrm{JudgePass}$ ), so the judge cannot on its own award a positive verdict, and judge passes that the deterministic layer fails are explicitly counted as failures. On the $5{,}012$ trials where both layers contributed verdicts, the two layers agree on the binary trial verdict $65.6\%$ of the time overall, and the judge concurs with deterministic-failure trials in $90.3\%$ of cases (CM $98.2\%$ , UM $89.6\%$ , PA $76.7\%$ ); the composite therefore rarely loses signal in the failure direction that drives the headline pass@ $k$ numbers in Table 2. (ii) Failure-mode dominance. Under the 7-category taxonomy (Appendix G), Harness-Fault accounts for only $1{.}0\%$ of analyzed non-passes; the residual $99{.}0\%$ concentrates in agent-attributable categories (Clinical-Reasoning, Workflow-Completion, Policy-Compliance, Tool-Use-Error, Abstain-or-Stuck, and Hallucination). The three judgment / completion / policy axes combined ( $71{.}9\%$ ) dominate the agent-attributable bucket, indicating that observed failures reflect agent execution and policy interpretation rather than verifier brittleness.

### G.1 Analysis methodology

We analyze all $5{,}886$ failed trials in Table 2 (30 (harness, model) cells $\times$ 25 tasks $\times$ 3 trials $\times$ 3 domains) according to the frozen 7-category taxonomy in Section G.2. The labelling pipeline has three tiers, applied in order; once a trial is assigned a first-level category and second-level mode it does not re-enter later tiers.

Tier 1: deterministic. A rule-based classifier reads each trial’s runtime logs (exception.txt, last tool call, step count, wall-clock budget) and the verifier outcome. It emits canonical labels for unambiguous cases: harness crash (sandbox crash, persistent 5xx, segfault), zero-step output (no actions before exit), wall-clock timeout (Modal/orchestrator CancelledError or DeepAgents AgentTimeoutError), fatal tool-call cascade (DeepAgents ToolException; classified as Tool-Use rather than infrastructure since the proximate cause is an agent-side malformed call that LangGraph’s default no-recovery policy escalates), success categories on rubric pass, and the unchanged Workflow-Completion top-level for trials whose rubric reports not_finalized without further ambiguity.

Tier 2: evidence-text classification. The remaining trials carry an analyzer-written natural-language summary from Section G.1 below. A second deterministic pass routes each summary based on substring matches: summaries that reference section / policy / wording / paraphrase / literal are labelled Policy-Compliance / criterion misreading; summaries that mention CM hard-refuse concern-mining, repeated re-framing, or pressured yes extraction are labelled Clinical-Reasoning / illegitimate consent; the residual ignored-condition-style cases route to Clinical-Reasoning / ignored clinical condition or action–narrative mismatch.

Tier 3: Trajectory verification. The trials whose analyzer evidence flags a candidate Hallucination (any fabricated-* mode) are re-checked end-to-end. Each trial’s persona prompt, full trajectory, and verifier outcome are passed to Claude Opus 4.7 with the boundary rule of Section G.2 and asked for a final first-level category and second-level mode plus $\geq 1$ verbatim patient-turn quote and $\geq 1$ verbatim agent-action quote. Trials whose verbatim evidence cannot establish an input-vs-output mismatch are demoted to Clinical-Reasoning / illegitimate consent (when the patient eventually said yes via concern-mining) or to Clinical-Reasoning / criteria misapplication. The verifier accepts $48$ trials as Hallucination (the strict cases where the structured field has no transcript support) and demotes the remaining $88$ to Clinical-Reasoning.

#### Analyzer.

The natural-language summaries used by Tier 2 are produced by Claude Opus 4.7 run once per trial against the full trial extract, the rubric outcome, and a 6-shot taxonomy example set. The analyzer returns a JSON record with the candidate first-level category, the candidate second-level mode, a supporting-evidence string, and a confidence label. The Tier 2 classifier consumes the supporting-evidence string; the candidate categories are used only as a fallback when the substring rules do not match.

## Abstract

How do Institutional Special Needs Plans (I-SNPs) affect end-of-life outcomes for nursing home residents with dementia?

In this cohort study of 1.4 million decedents with dementia who died in nursing homes between 2013 and 2022, I-SNP enrollees had significantly lower rates of hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, and mechanical ventilation in the last month of life, but no differences in hospice use, compared to decedents not enrolled in I-SNP.

## Abstract

Nursing home residents with dementia are often unnecessarily hospitalized at the end of life. Institutional Special Needs Plans (I-SNPs) are a type of Medicare Advantage plan for long-term nursing home residents that use advanced practice clinicians to manage care. Studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of the original and largest I-SNP operated by UnitedHealthcare (UHC), but there has been minimal evaluation of non-UHC I-SNPs, which have driven recent growth, nor specific focus on end-of-life outcomes.

To examine the association of I-SNP enrollment with end-of-life outcomes for nursing home residents with dementia, separately for UHC and non-UHC I-SNPs.

This retrospective cohort study used 2010 to 2022 Medicare data on 1.4 million long-stay nursing home residents with dementia who died between 2013 and 2022. Facility-level and patient-level selection bias were addressed with cross-temporal propensity score matching and difference-in-differences models. Both the direct effects of I-SNP enrollment, as well as the indirect (ie, spillover) effects on nonenrollees residing in nursing homes offering I-SNPs were assessed. Variation in these relationships by I-SNP maturity was also examined. Data were analyzed from November 2024 to April 2026.

Four I-SNP exposure categories: UHC I-SNP enrollment and spillover; non-UHC I-SNP enrollment and spillover.

Hospitalization and hospice use in the last month of life.

The study cohort included 1 415 265 long-stay nursing home residents with dementia who died between 2013 and 2022. The unadjusted hospitalization rate in the last 30 days of life was 27.7%. UHC I-SNP enrollment was associated with a 9.0–percentage point (pp) reduction in hospitalization (95% CI, −10.3 pp to −7.7 pp) while non-UHC I-SNP enrollment was associated with a 5.9-pp reduction (95% CI, −8.4 pp to −3.5 pp). The spillover effect on nonenrollees in nursing homes offering a UHC I-SNP was a 1.7-pp (95% CI, −2.4 pp to −1.1 pp) decline in hospitalizations; the spillover effect in non-UHC nursing homes was not statistically significant. Similar trends appeared with hospitalization in the last 3 days of life, intensive care unit admission, and mechanical ventilation, but there was no association with hospice use. The reduction in hospitalizations increased in the 3 years after nursing home I-SNP adoption, then plateaued.

In this retrospective cohort study, I-SNP enrollment was associated with significantly fewer hospitalizations for nursing home residents with dementia at the end of life, with effect sizes larger for UHC vs non-UHC I-SNPs. Plan maturity and volume are likely important factors impacting success.

## Abstract

This cohort study evaluates the association between Institutional Special Needs Plan enrollment and end-of-life outcomes using Medicare data for 1.4 million nursing home residents with dementia who died between 2013 and 2022.

## Introduction

Nursing home residents with dementia often face burdensome interventions at the end of life, including hospitalization and intensive care unit (ICU) admission.1,2,3 Contributing factors include limited on-site medical staff, inadequate capacity to perform timely diagnostics or initiate treatments such as intravenous therapy, and insufficient advance care planning.1,3 Furthermore, Medicare’s 3-day hospitalization rule to qualify for Part A skilled care incentivizes nursing homes to hospitalize acutely ill long-stay residents, even if they could be safely treated in place, so that those residents might then get readmitted to the nursing home under Part A, generating higher reimbursement than the facility would receive if they initiated skilled treatments like intravenous therapy under Medicare Part B. Low reimbursement rates under Medicaid for long-stay residents further increase financial incentive for nursing homes to hospitalize those residents to recoup Part A skilled payments upon readmission.

The Institutional Special Needs Plan (I-SNP) model, a type of Medicare Advantage (MA) plan for long-term nursing home residents, aims to address these issues. I-SNPs are rooted in the Evercare model, which was developed by 2 Minnesota nurse practitioners to improve medical care coordination in nursing homes.4,5 That model, designated as a Medicare demonstration in 1987, has operated under UnitedHealthcare (UHC) ever since.4,5 Following the initial success of the Evercare demonstration,6,7,8,9,10 the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) formally authorized I-SNPs in 2003.11 The core I-SNP elements today remain unchanged. I-SNPs contract with nursing homes, and then the plans enroll long-stay residents in those facilities, meaning that only residents of participating nursing homes are eligible. I-SNPs receive capitated risk-adjusted Medicare payments and must operate a CMS-approved model of care to facilitate care management. Plans employ advanced practice clinicians (nurse practitioners and physician assistants) to collaborate with nursing home nursing staff and physicians to coordinate care, manage chronic conditions, treat acute illness, and lead advanced care planning.6,7 Additionally, I-SNPs waive Medicare’s 3-day hospitalization rule, and pay nursing homes a Part A rate when residents meet skilled criteria for changes in condition that are treated in-house. Plans also offer various value-based payment mechanisms in their contracts with nursing homes as incentives to meet quality targets. These can range from quality incentive payments for specific outcomes to shared-savings contracts in which nursing homes share financial risk with the I-SNP.

There has been substantial growth and diversification of I-SNPs over the last 2 decades.11,12,13 This growth is likely attributed to both the clinical success of the model as well as the potential for nursing homes to capture more revenue through their capitated contracts. Although the UHC I-SNP (since renamed from Evercare to Optum CarePlus) remains the oldest and largest I-SNP, more recent growth has been driven by non-UHC plans. Existing evidence on I-SNPs comes primarily from the UHC model, which has been associated with reduced hospitalizations, higher family satisfaction, and more advance directive completion.7,8,9,10,14,15 However, most of those studies are more than 20 years old and do not fully account for selection bias that may occur if plans enroll healthier individuals. More recent studies have examined I-SNP effectiveness more generally, inclusive of both UHC and non-UHC plans, and have identified similar reductions in hospitalizations but mixed benefits for other outcomes.11,16,17,18,19

Given the maturity and market dominance of the UHC I-SNP, there is a need to assess the performance of UHC and non-UHC plans separately. Additionally, no studies have examined how I-SNPs impact end-of-life outcomes such as hospitalization, intensive care use, and hospice use, all of which may be particularly sensitive to this model and have substantial relevance for delivering high-quality dementia care in nursing homes. I-SNP clinicians are expected to facilitate care coordination, advance care planning, and provide palliative care,6,14 but how I-SNPs work with hospice is less understood.19 I-SNPs also bring certain resources to nursing homes that may impact care for all residents, not just those who enroll. For example, I-SNP clinicians typically mentor nursing staff in nursing homes; while plans often require timely pharmacy, laboratory, and radiology services to be in place to support treatment-in-place. Potential spillover effects of I-SNP on nonenrollees in nursing homes that offer I-SNPs have not previously been characterized. Finally, because it takes time to build the necessary infrastructure to support successful I-SNP enrollment and operation in a nursing home, the maturity of an I-SNP in a nursing home is an important dimension warranting further investigation.

In this study, we examined associations of I-SNP enrollment with hospitalization and hospice use for nursing home residents with dementia at the end of life. We examined UHC and non-UHC I-SNPs separately, using a cross-temporal propensity score matching approach to address potential selection bias in whom plans enroll. Additionally, we assessed both the direct effects of I-SNP enrollment, as well as the spillover effects on nonenrollees who lived in nursing homes where an I-SNP was operating. Finally, we assessed whether years of I-SNP maturity within an nursing home were associated with person-level outcomes.

## Methods

This retrospective cohort study was approved by the Brown University Institutional Review Board, which waived the need for informed consent due to the use of deidentified claims data. The study follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline.

### Data Sources

We used 2010 to 2022 Medicare data, including the Master Beneficiary Summary File (MBSF), Medicare Provider Analysis and Review (MedPAR) files, and hospice claims. The MBSF includes beneficiary demographics, date of death, and monthly indicators of Medicaid eligibility and MA plan enrollment, including contract numbers and plan IDs. We classified MA plans as I-SNPs using CMS special needs plan data.20 For both traditional Medicare and MA enrollees, MedPAR captures hospitalization data while hospice claims capture hospice episodes. We used the nursing home Minimum Data Set (MDS) to identify long-stay nursing home residents and measure clinical characteristics.

### Study Population

The study population included all Medicare beneficiaries with dementia who were long-term nursing home residents (ie, admitted for ≥100 days) and died between January 1, 2013, and December 31, 2022. We identified dementia from MedPAR and MDS diagnosis codes, applying the Bynum-Standard algorithm.21 Fourteen states with few or no nursing homes participating in I-SNPs were excluded (eTable 1 in Supplement 1).

### Variables

#### I-SNP Exposure

Individuals may be directly exposed to an I-SNP through enrollment, or indirectly exposed through spillover effects when residing in an nursing home that offers an I-SNP. We thus classified decedents into 4 treatment categories reflecting both facility-level and person-level I-SNP exposure: (1) UHC I-SNP enrollees, (2) non-UHC I-SNP enrollees, (3) nonenrollees in facilities offering a UHC I-SNP (spillover), and (4) nonenrollees in facilities offering a non-UHC I-SNP (spillover).

For all long-stay residents, we determined UHC and non-UHC I-SNP enrollment in each month, then counted resident-months by facility, for each I-SNP type. We classified nursing homes as participating with an I-SNP in a given year if they had at least 5 I-SNP enrollee-months involving 2 or more unique enrollees (determined separately for UHC vs non-UHC). This yielded a facility-year panel from 2010 to 2022, allowing identification of the first year of I-SNP adoption, as well as pretrends and posttrends. Decedents were classified as I-SNP enrollees if they were enrolled for at least 2 of the last 3 months of life.

#### Outcomes

The primary outcomes were hospitalization in the last 30 days and 3 days of life. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation, ICU admission, and hospice use during the last 30 days of life.

#### Covariates

Age, sex, race and ethnicity, Medicaid eligibility, and MA plan enrollment were all determined as of the date the person became a long-term nursing home resident. We also included the count of days from becoming a long-term nursing home resident to date of death, as well as activities of daily living and cognitive function scores22 from the MDS assessment closest to death. Race and ethnicity data were obtained from the MBSF self-reported categories modified by the Research Triangle Institute algorithm, which uses first and last names to enhance race and ethnicity designation. The categories include American Indian and Alaska Native, Asian and Pacific Islander, Black or African American, Hispanic, non-Hispanic White, other, and unknown.

### Statistical Analysis

Analytically, the I-SNP treatment is a 2-step process: (1) nursing homes select to contract or not with an I-SNP plan (so potentially all their residents experience some level of treatment), and (2) residents in I-SNP nursing homes enroll or not in I-SNP. For this reason, we performed 2 main types of analyses. First, we estimated the overall effect of nursing home I-SNP adoption on I-SNP enrollment, and on decedents’ outcomes. These models included all decedents in each nursing home, enrolled or not in I-SNP, and compared outcomes before and after nursing homes adopted I-SNPs, with separate indicators for UHC vs non-UHC I-SNP adoption. Models adjusted for resident-level covariates, calendar year–quarter fixed effects, and nursing home fixed effects. To examine dynamic effects and assess pretreatment trends, we also estimated staggered difference-in-differences models using the calendar year prior to I-SNP adoption as the reference category, with indicators for preadoption (–4 to –1) and postadoption (1 to ≥5) years. In these intention-to-treat analyses, nursing homes that never adopted an I-SNP contributed to identifying secular trends.

The second type of analyses allows us to disentangle the direct effects for I-SNP enrollees from the indirect (spillover) effects on nonenrolled residents in I-SNP facilities. To address the selective nature of person-level enrollment, we applied a cross-temporal propensity score matching approach,23,24 described in detail in eMethods in Supplement 1. Briefly, the method improves over cross-sectional matching (where nonenrollees can be substantially different from those who enroll) by matching to similar individuals in the facility in pretreatment, where persons likely to enroll or not are all observed without treatment. For each resident in each of the 4 treatment groups (UHC I-SNP enrollees, non-UHC I-SNP enrollees, nonenrollees in facilities with the UHC I-SNP, nonenrollees in facilities with a non-UHC I-SNP), we identified 3 matched controls: (1) a decedent who died in an I-SNP facility but in a year before the facility offered I-SNP; (2) a decedent who died in the same year as the treated individual in a facility that never offered I-SNP; and (3) a decedent who died in the same year as the first control individual in a facility that never offered I-SNP. The difference in outcomes between the treated individual and the first control individual reflects a combined effect of I-SNP exposure and time trend, as the control died in a different year. The difference in outcomes between the second and third control individuals provides the time trend effect estimate to isolate the I-SNP treatment effect in the difference-in-differences model. Using this balanced cross-temporal matched cohort, we conducted the difference-in-differences estimation, including all patient covariates and match-identifier fixed effects to adjust for residual matching imbalance. Finally, we estimated a staggered-treatment version of this difference-in-differences model using the same year indicators described in the previous paragraph, measuring years before and after nursing home I-SNP adoption. This allowed us to assess for pretrends and examine the effects of plan maturity within a facility on both the enrollment and spillover effects. Data were analyzed from November 2024 to April 2026 using Stata MP, version 19.0 (StataCorp LLC).

## Discussion

The findings of this retrospective cohort study suggest that the I-SNP model is an important intervention for improving end-of-life care to nursing home residents with dementia. Accounting for selection bias in whom plans enroll, we observed that I-SNP enrollment was associated with significant reduction in hospitalizations, ICU admissions, and mechanical ventilation at the end of life, with effect sizes being slightly larger for UHC vs non-UHC plans. I-SNP enrollment was not associated with hospice use, potentially because I-SNP clinicians are already managing palliative care needs, but more work is needed to understand that relationship.

We further identified that UHC I-SNPs had spillover effects on nonenrollees who resided in nursing homes with those plans, while the non-UHC spillover effects were not statistically significant except for mechanical ventilation. With the UHC spillover effects, we observed a more sizeable reduction in hospitalizations with longer plan maturity within a facility. This could be due to a few underlying mechanisms. I-SNPs often require that nursing homes have infrastructure in place, like timely laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy services, intravenous supplies, and various stocked medications, resources that are then available for use on all patients. Furthermore, I-SNP quality incentives combined with the presence of an I-SNP clinician may help to facilitate broader culture change and staff preparedness in an nursing home around palliative care, advance care planning, and treatment-in-place of acute illness. While we examined how I-SNP maturity within an nursing home contributes to variation in spillover effects in this study, other important factors, such as maturity and volume at the market and plan levels, likely also contribute to spillover heterogeneity and may explain the differences we observed in UHC vs non-UHC plans.

The maturity of the relationship between an I-SNP and nursing home also appears to influence outcomes. While the current study focuses on end-of-life outcomes, these maturity effects are similar to those seen in prior work examining hospitalizations in the broader long-stay population.25 I-SNPs require complex infrastructure to manage and integrate the financial and clinical components of the model successfully. Plans must enroll and maintain enough participant volume both within nursing homes and across their markets to manage financial risk. The UHC I-SNP has a first-mover advantage, which has given it more time than other plans to grow its footprint and refine necessary administrative, technological, and clinical structures and processes. Advanced practice clinicians are at the core of the I-SNP model, but they must have sufficient patient panels within nursing homes to support them being regularly present and influential over care. When an I-SNP clinician must manage smaller panels across multiple nursing homes, they cannot visit each facility as often and thus are less available to residents, family, and staff.

Our findings suggest that there is, on average, approximately a 2-year transition period after nursing home I-SNP adoption before that facility reaches a steady state of enrolled participants. During that period, the nursing home’s staff, physicians, residents, and families are becoming familiar with the I-SNP clinician and model, and the facility may need to build its clinical capacity. We observed a larger maturity effect with UHC vs non-UHC I-SNPs, potentially suggesting that UHC has refined the necessary processes and structures to open new nursing homes with rapid model implementation, whereas other plans may experience more of a learning curve in earlier years. Our findings build on a recent study that examined nursing homes with mature vs no I-SNPs,16 by examining outcomes during that transition period, and assessing differences between UHC and non-UHC I-SNPs.

### Limitations

This study has limitations. First, we determined whether an nursing home had a relationship with an I-SNP based on patient enrollment records, rather than direct measures of contracts between nursing homes and I-SNPs, which were unavailable, meaning there could be some measurement error in our specification. Second, there may be some measurement error in our claims-based identification of dementia diagnoses, though we would expect this error to be random across the study population. Third, we categorized I-SNPs as UHC vs non-UHC, as this was the natural grouping given plan volume and patient enrollment; however, there is inherent heterogeneity in the non-UHC category, and further work is needed to disentangle differences between plans within that group.

## Conclusions

In this retrospective cohort study, I-SNP enrollment was associated with a significant reduction in hospitalizations for nursing home residents with dementia in the last month of life, suggesting that the I-SNP model is an important intervention for minimizing burdensome interventions at the end of life for this population. It is critical to continue monitoring I-SNP growth and quality outcomes closely, particularly as the landscape of I-SNP plans becomes increasingly heterogeneous.
